historical_timeline.summary: Born Walker Smith Jr. (Ailey, Georgia, or Detroit, by different sources).
Wins the Golden Gloves featherweight title after moving to Harlem.
Boxes professionally for 25 years, about 200 bouts.
Wins the world welterweight title; later holds the middleweight title five times, first in 1951.
Founds the Sugar Ray Robinson Youth Foundation in Los Angeles.
Reported to have Alzheimer's disease, diabetes and hypertension.
Dies at 67 at Brotman Medical Center in Culver City.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Mild dementia due to early-onset Alzheimer's disease in a 63-year-old retired boxer with type 2 diabetes and hypertension, seen in Los Angeles with his care partner. The episode follows the 1982 Alzheimer's Association DETeCD-ADRD guideline: a structured history from him and an informant, the MoCA, MMSE and CDR, function, reversible causes (B12, TSH, depression, anticholinergic medicines, sleep apnea and hearing), brain MRI, and amyloid PET to confirm the cause; how Alzheimer's disease differs from traumatic encephalopathy syndrome, a research diagnosis for people with long exposure to repetitive head impacts; why he is not a candidate for lecanemab or donanemab under the appropriate use recommendations (more than four cerebral microbleeds), and why APOE genotyping was not needed for that decision; donepezil, its pulse and stomach side effects, and a dose step back; deintensifying diabetes treatment under the ADA Standards for older adults (stopping the sulfonylurea; a goal under 8.0%) with sick-day rules for metformin; blood pressure; driving and firearm safety; hearing aids; caregiver support, respite and the Medicare GUIDE model he may join once on Medicare; and advance care planning while he can take part.

visit_schedule.purpose: Establishing care for memory loss and getting lost, with his care partner: cognitive testing, reversible causes, medicines, diabetes and blood pressure, driving and firearm safety

Six-week review: amyloid PET result, the diagnosis and the plan, with diabetes, driving, firearm and caregiver support
Eleven-week review: donepezil dose, diabetes, hearing aids and day program
Same-day sick visit for nausea and dizziness on donepezil
Sixteen-week review: medicines, kidneys, mood, caregiver strain and the plan

hpi.narrative: Sugar Ray Robinson returns two weeks after intake with his care partner and is seen the same day by Dr. Haddad-Kowalski at the memory clinic. He had a brain MRI and a hearing test this morning. His intake blood count, kidney function, B12 and TSH were normal; hemoglobin A1c was 6.4%. He has slept well since stopping the over-the-counter sleep aid. He has not driven since intake; his care partner drives. The handgun stays unloaded and locked with the key held by his care partner. He repeated one question twice during the visit and laughed about it.

assessment_plan.assessment: Dr. Haddad-Kowalski finds mild dementia (CDR 1, MMSE 22) with an amnestic pattern and hippocampal atrophy, most likely due to Alzheimer's disease; long exposure to repetitive head impacts raises traumatic encephalopathy syndrome, a research diagnosis, as a contributor; vascular change is slight. Reversible causes have been excluded or treated. The six microbleeds rule out lecanemab and donanemab under the appropriate use recommendations, so APOE genotyping is not needed for that decision. An amyloid PET will confirm or exclude Alzheimer's disease, which he wants to know

referral.question: Two years of progressive memory loss with getting lost while driving in a retired professional boxer of 63 with type 2 diabetes and hypertension; MoCA 18. Please stage the impairment, weigh Alzheimer's disease against traumatic encephalopathy syndrome and vascular disease, advise on biomarker testing and on eligibility for anti-amyloid therapy, and help us plan safety and support
referral.urgency: Routine; at the memory clinic two weeks from now, on the same day as his two-week primary care visit, with brain MRI and audiometry that morning
referral.pertinent_history: Retired world champion boxer: about 200 professional bouts over 25 years after an amateur career. Memory loss for about two years, worse in the past six months: repeated questions, missed bills and appointments, and lost twice in familiar streets while driving. Independent in personal care; needs help with finances and medicines (Functional Activities Questionnaire 11). MoCA 18 with losses in delayed recall, orientation and executive tasks; PHQ-9 4. About ten years of schooling. Diabetes on metformin and glipizide (hemoglobin A1c 6.4%); hypertension on lisinopril; atorvastatin. Diphenhydramine 25 mg nightly stopped today. Blood count, metabolic panel (creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, eGFR 85), B12 352 pg/mL and TSH 1.9 normal; urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 14 mg/g. STOP-Bang 2. No anticoagulant. He has agreed not to drive until the work-up is done; a handgun at home is unloaded and locked with the key held by his care partner, who comes to visits
questions: What is the stage of his impairment, and is the pattern most consistent with Alzheimer's disease?
How should we think about traumatic encephalopathy syndrome and chronic traumatic encephalopathy after his boxing career, and about vascular disease?
Which biomarker test do you advise, and should APOE genotyping be done?
Is he a candidate for lecanemab or donanemab under the appropriate use recommendations?
What do you advise for symptomatic treatment, driving, firearm safety, hearing and support for his care partner?

consultant_note.history: Sugar Ray Robinson, a retired professional boxer of 63, is seen at the memory clinic with his care partner at the request of Dr. Pryce-Okonjo. He says his memory is not what it was but that this is normal at his age; his care partner describes two years of slowly worsening forgetfulness for recent events, repeated questions and stories, missed bills, and two episodes of getting lost while driving in familiar streets. There has been no sudden change, no hallucinations, no acting out of dreams, no falls and no change in personality, temper or mood. He boxed for about 25 years; he remembers many hard fights but cannot say how often he was dazed. He exercises daily and still goes to the gym of the youth foundation he started
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Pryce-Okonjo's intake note. MoCA 18 at intake (education point included); PHQ-9 4; Functional Activities Questionnaire 11. Blood count, metabolic panel, B12, TSH and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio normal; hemoglobin A1c 6.4%. Brain MRI this morning: moderate bilateral hippocampal atrophy, left more than right, mild generalized atrophy, Fazekas 1 white matter change, six microbleeds at the gray-white junction of both frontal lobes and the right temporal lobe, no cortical superficial siderosis or infarct, and a cavum septi pellucidi. Audiometry this morning: mild to moderate bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. No anticoagulant or antiplatelet drug. Today: MMSE 22; global CDR 1, sum of boxes 5.5

exam.finding: Cranial nerves normal; no rigidity, tremor, bradykinesia or dysarthria; normal strength, reflexes and coordination; steady narrow-based gait
Alert and courteous; repeats questions; impaired delayed recall that cueing helps little; mild executive slowing; language and visuospatial copying preserved; no psychotic symptoms

assessment.assessment: Mild dementia (global CDR 1, MMSE 22, MoCA 18) with an amnestic presentation and progressive course, independent in personal care but dependent for complex tasks. With bilateral hippocampal atrophy, this is most consistent with Alzheimer's disease beginning before 65. Depression, thyroid disease, B12 deficiency and anticholinergic drugs have been excluded or addressed; sleep apnea risk is low; hearing loss is a treatable contributor

assessment.display: Traumatic encephalopathy syndrome and vascular disease
assessment.assessment: Twenty-five years of professional boxing is substantial exposure to repetitive head impacts. Under the 1979 NINDS consensus criteria, traumatic encephalopathy syndrome is a research diagnosis for people with that exposure and progressive cognitive or neurobehavioral impairment; it is not meant to guide routine clinical care, and the underlying disease, chronic traumatic encephalopathy, can be confirmed only after death. He has no neurobehavioral dysregulation or parkinsonism, and the amnestic pattern with hippocampal atrophy points to Alzheimer's disease; repetitive head impacts may still add to his difficulty, as the microbleeds and cavum septi pellucidi suggest past injury. Vascular change is slight and does not explain his dementia

Confirming Alzheimer's pathology will settle the diagnosis, which he wants, inform counseling and planning, and distinguish it from a mainly traumatic process. Amyloid PET is the test I advise. APOE genotyping informs the risk of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities for anti-amyloid therapy; since he is not a candidate, it would not change his care, and it carries implications for relatives. It can be offered with genetic counseling if he wishes

By stage and MMSE (20 to 30 for donanemab, 22 to 30 for lecanemab) he would otherwise fit, and he takes no anticoagulant. But both the lecanemab and donanemab appropriate use recommendations exclude people with more than four cerebral microbleeds on the pre-treatment MRI because of the risk of bleeding and amyloid-related imaging abnormalities. With six microbleeds he does not qualify, whatever his amyloid status

Hemoglobin A1c 6.4% on glipizide is tighter than needed: for an older adult with cognitive impairment the ADA Standards advise a goal under 8.0% and avoiding drugs that cause hypoglycemia, which harms memory and raises the risk of falls. Blood pressure is well controlled

If amyloid is confirmed, a cholinesterase inhibitor offers modest benefit: donepezil 5 mg, then 10 mg after four to six weeks if tolerated, after a baseline ECG, watching for nausea, loose stools, vivid dreams and a slow pulse. Memantine is for moderate dementia. With CDR 1 and getting lost while driving, his driving risk is high and he should not drive. A firearm should not be kept in the home of a person with dementia. Hearing aids, exercise, social activity and support for his care partner, including respite, matter as much as medicine

recommendations: Amyloid PET to confirm Alzheimer's disease pathology; disclosure of the result with his care partner present if he wishes
Not a candidate for lecanemab or donanemab: more than four microbleeds on MRI; APOE genotyping not needed for treatment and offered only with genetic counseling
Traumatic encephalopathy syndrome recorded as a consideration only; it is a research diagnosis and does not change treatment

If amyloid is positive: donepezil 5 mg after a baseline ECG, raised to 10 mg after four to six weeks if tolerated; step back to 5 mg, or take it in the morning, for nausea, diarrhea, vivid dreams or a slow pulse
Stop glipizide and keep metformin, with a hemoglobin A1c goal under 8.0%
No driving; remove the firearm from the home
Care partner education and respite, with the Alzheimer's Association 24/7 Helpline and an adult day program; the GUIDE dementia care model once he has Medicare
Advance care planning soon, while he can take part fully
MoCA and CDR yearly, or sooner with change; repeat MRI only for an acute change

provenance_review.notes: Sources: UPI obituary (1989), UPI report of a Sports Illustrated article (1987), the Michigan Sports Hall of Fame, the West Adams Heritage Association and Boxing News. The International Boxing Hall of Fame site refused connection; the New York Times and Los Angeles Times obituaries could not be fetched; Wil Haygood's Sweet Thunder was not read. The birthplace is disputed (Ailey, Georgia, or Detroit), and record counts differ by source. No source dates his Alzheimer's diagnosis.

safe_messaging_review.notes: Dementia claims use only the documented press reports (Alzheimer's disease, diabetes, hypertension in 1987; Alzheimer's disease and diabetes at his death) and are marked sensitive. Dementia pugilistica and chronic traumatic encephalopathy are recorded only as an R roster claim. No relative is named in the modern episode; the care partner is synthetic, unnamed and not modeled on any relative, and family disputes in the 1987 report are not used.
